blocks.robotComment: Everything so far in this app lives in one bucket. This track is entirely about the other one. 🗂️
blocks.body: Traditional assets are the well-established categories most people build their financial foundation on: stocks, bonds, funds, and real estate, all covered elsewhere in this app. Alternative assets are everything outside that traditional core — cryptocurrency, commodities like gold, collectibles, and private investments like venture capital.

Alternative assets generally share a few traits: they're often more volatile, harder to value precisely, less regulated, and less liquid (harder to quickly convert to cash) than traditional assets. That doesn't automatically make them bad — it makes them a different kind of tool, best used carefully and in the right proportion.

blocks.sentence: Categories outside the traditional core of stocks, bonds, funds, and real estate are generally called ___ assets.
blocks.explanation: Anything outside the well-established traditional categories — like crypto, commodities, and collectibles — falls under the alternative-assets umbrella.

blocks.robotComment: This whole track is written with a caution-first mindset — this isn't a pitch to buy anything. 🧭
blocks.body: This track is written deliberately cautiously. Alternative assets attract a lot of hype, and hype has burned a lot of people who bought in for the wrong reasons at the wrong moment. The goal here is real understanding — enough to make an informed, deliberate decision about whether and how much exposure, if any, makes sense for you — not a pitch to buy anything specific.

blocks.question: What generally distinguishes alternative assets from traditional ones?
options: They tend to be more volatile, harder to value, less regulated, and less liquid
They are always a better investment
They are guaranteed to lose money
They are identical to traditional assets in every way
blocks.explanation: These traits don't make alternative assets bad, but they do mean they generally require extra caution and understanding.

blocks.statement: This track's goal is to convince you to buy cryptocurrency or other alternative assets.
blocks.explanation: The goal is informed understanding so you can make your own deliberate decision, not a sales pitch for any specific asset.

blocks.robotComment: Strip away the hype and the jargon, and the core idea is actually pretty simple. 🔗
blocks.body: Cryptocurrency is a form of digital money built on a blockchain: a shared, continuously growing digital record of transactions, maintained by a network of computers instead of a single bank or government. Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was the first, and thousands of others have followed since.

The key difference from a traditional bank account is who's in control. A bank maintains its own private record of your balance, and can freeze or reverse transactions. A blockchain's record is shared across a distributed network, with no single company or government in charge of it — that's what people mean by decentralization, covered in more depth next level.

highlights.text: no single company or government in charge

blocks.sentence: Cryptocurrency is built on a ___: a shared, continuously growing digital record maintained by a network instead of one bank.
blocks.explanation: A blockchain is the shared, decentralized ledger technology that cryptocurrency is built on top of.

blocks.robotComment: Decentralization is genuinely interesting technology — that's separate from whether any given coin is a good investment. ⚠️
blocks.body: It's worth separating two different questions early: whether the underlying technology is genuinely interesting (it is, and this track explores why) and whether any specific cryptocurrency is a good investment for you (a much harder, more personal question, covered honestly in later levels). Plenty of interesting technology has still made for a poor short-term investment, and vice versa.

blocks.question: What is the key difference between how a bank tracks your balance and how a blockchain works?
options: A blockchain's record is shared across a distributed network with no single controlling party, unlike a bank's private ledger
Blockchains and banks work in an identical way
A blockchain only exists on one company's private server
Banks use blockchains for every single account
blocks.explanation: Decentralization — no single party controlling the record — is the defining technical difference from a traditional bank's private ledger.

blocks.statement: Whether a technology is genuinely interesting and whether a specific cryptocurrency is a good investment are the exact same question.
blocks.explanation: These are two separate questions — interesting technology doesn't automatically make any specific coin a good investment, and this track treats them separately.

lessons.title: Why Alternative Assets Attract Attention — and Why to Be Careful

blocks.robotComment: The stories that go viral are never the boring, typical ones. Keep that in mind for this whole track. 📢
blocks.body: Alternative assets, especially cryptocurrency, attract enormous attention because of dramatic stories: someone who bought early and became wealthy, a rare collectible that sold for a fortune, a commodity that spiked overnight. These stories spread because they're exciting, not because they're typical.

This creates a real bias in what you hear about: the rare, spectacular winners get talked about constantly, while the far more common losses, stagnation, or projects that simply disappeared get almost no attention at all. Level 9 of this track covers this exact pattern — survivorship bias — in much more depth.

blocks.sentence: The tendency to only hear about the rare, spectacular winners — not the common losses — is related to a pattern called survivorship ___.
blocks.explanation: Survivorship bias describes exactly this: attention concentrates on visible winners while the much larger group of losses stays invisible.

blocks.robotComment: None of this means alternative assets are worthless — it just means the loud stories deserve real skepticism. 🧠
blocks.body: None of this means alternative assets have no value or place in a thoughtful financial plan — Levels 5 through 7 explore commodities, collectibles, and reasonable position sizing in real depth. It just means the loudest, most exciting stories are the least representative ones, and deserve real skepticism rather than automatic belief.

blocks.question: Why do dramatic stories about alternative assets spread so widely?
options: Exciting, unusual stories get shared far more than typical or boring outcomes
They are always accurate and representative
They are required by law to be publicized
Boring outcomes never happen with alternative assets
blocks.explanation: What spreads widely is what's exciting, not what's typical — which is exactly why these stories can be misleading if taken at face value.

blocks.statement: The dramatic success stories heard about alternative assets are generally representative of the typical outcome.
blocks.explanation: The loudest stories are the rare, exciting outliers — the much more common typical or losing outcomes get far less attention.

lessons.title: What a Blockchain Actually Is, Simply

blocks.robotComment: Think of it less like a filing cabinet and more like the same notebook, copied identically onto thousands of desks at once. 📒
blocks.body: A blockchain is a shared, continuously growing record of transactions, copied across thousands of separate computers instead of sitting on one company's server. Each new batch of transactions, called a block, gets linked to the one before it, forming a chain stretching all the way back to the very first entry.

highlights.text: linked to the one before it

blocks.body: The append-only part matters as much as the shared part. New blocks can be added onto the end of the chain, but old blocks essentially can't be secretly rewritten, because every computer in the network holds its own copy, and a change that doesn't match everyone else's copy gets rejected.

blocks.sentence: A blockchain is a shared, ___ record of transactions replicated across many computers.
blocks.explanation: Append-only means new blocks can be added, but existing ones can't be secretly rewritten without the rest of the network noticing.

blocks.robotComment: No single copy gets to be the official one that's quietly edited — that's the whole point. 🔒
blocks.body: This is also why blockchains are often described as tamper-evident rather than tamper-proof: someone could theoretically try to alter a copy, but doing so undetected would require simultaneously changing the matching copies held by a huge number of independent computers, which becomes wildly impractical as the network grows.

blocks.question: What makes a blockchain different from a normal spreadsheet stored on one server?
options: It's copied across many independent computers, and old entries can't easily be rewritten without the network noticing
It can only ever be viewed by one company
It automatically deletes old transactions after a year
It requires no computers at all to maintain
blocks.explanation: The defining features are replication across many independent computers and the practical difficulty of secretly rewriting history.

blocks.statement: A blockchain's record is typically stored on a single company's private server.
blocks.explanation: The whole point of a blockchain is that the record is replicated across many independent computers, not centralized on one server.

lessons.title: Decentralization: What It Means and Why It Matters

blocks.robotComment: Compare that to a bank, which absolutely can freeze your account or reverse a transaction with a single decision. 🏦
blocks.body: Decentralization means no single person, company, or government controls the network or can unilaterally change its rules. Thousands of independent computers, called nodes, each keep a full copy of the record and agree on updates using a shared set of rules, rather than deferring to one central authority.

highlights.text: no single person, company, or government controls the network

blocks.body: One practical benefit is resilience: because the record isn't stored in one place, there's no single point of failure. Governments and companies can't easily shut it down by unplugging one server, and the network typically keeps running even if a large number of individual computers go offline at once.

blocks.robotComment: This is a genuine tradeoff, not a flaw to be embarrassed about — speed and easy fixes get traded for resilience and no single point of control. ⚖️
blocks.body: Decentralization isn't free, though, and it's worth being honest about the tradeoffs. Getting thousands of independent computers to agree slows things down — a decentralized network is typically much slower and more expensive per transaction than a centralized database run by one company. There's also no customer service line to call: if you make a mistake, there's usually no central authority able to reverse it for you.

highlights.text: typically much slower and more expensive
no central authority able to reverse it for you

blocks.sentence: No single person, company, or government controlling a network is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Decentralization is spreading control across many independent participants instead of one central authority.

blocks.question: Which of these is an honest tradeoff of decentralization?
options: It typically makes transactions slower and more expensive than a centralized system, in exchange for no single point of control or failure
It means a central company can reverse any mistake instantly
It guarantees a cryptocurrency's price will rise
blocks.explanation: Decentralization trades speed and convenience for resilience and the absence of a single controlling party — both sides are real.

blocks.statement: Decentralization means there are no real costs or tradeoffs compared to a centralized system.
blocks.explanation: Decentralized networks are typically slower and more expensive to run per transaction, and mistakes usually can't be reversed by a central authority — real tradeoffs for real benefits.

blocks.robotComment: Different blockchains use different methods here — the goal is always the same, even when the mechanics vary. ⚙️
blocks.body: Before a transaction gets added to the blockchain, the network has to agree it's legitimate — that the sender actually has the funds and hasn't already spent them elsewhere. This confirmation process is often called mining or validation, depending on the specific blockchain, and it's what turns a pending transaction into a permanent part of the record.

Two common approaches exist. In proof of work, computers called miners compete to solve a difficult puzzle, and whoever solves it first gets to add the next block and earn a reward — this is the original approach, used by Bitcoin, and it consumes a significant amount of computing power and electricity. In proof of stake, validators instead lock up some of their own cryptocurrency as a deposit, known as staking, and the network selects among them to confirm the next block, using far less energy.
Here's a simplified look at what a miner or validator is actually rewarded for.

code.code:
New block contains 500 pending transactions
Miner/validator checks that each one is valid
Block gets added to the chain
Miner/validator receives a reward: newly created coins + transaction fees
code.caption: The reward is what motivates thousands of independent computers to keep validating honestly.

blocks.sentence: The process of confirming transactions and adding them permanently to a blockchain is often called mining or ___.
blocks.explanation: Validation (or mining, depending on the blockchain) is what confirms transactions are legitimate before they become permanent.

blocks.question: What is the basic difference between proof of work and proof of stake, conceptually?
options: Proof of work has miners compete by solving puzzles using computing power; proof of stake has validators lock up cryptocurrency instead
They are exactly the same process under two different names
Proof of stake requires far more electricity than proof of work
blocks.explanation: Both aim to confirm transactions honestly, but proof of work relies on computing power and proof of stake relies on locked-up cryptocurrency as a deposit.

blocks.statement: Validators or miners are typically rewarded in some way for confirming transactions correctly.
blocks.explanation: A reward, usually newly created coins and/or transaction fees, is what motivates the network to keep validating honestly.
blocks.robotComment: That reward is also exactly why mining and staking became businesses in their own right. 💰

chapters.title: Keys, Wallets, and Who's In Control

blocks.robotComment: This one distinction explains most of the risk and convenience tradeoffs in the rest of this level. 🔑
blocks.body: A cryptocurrency wallet doesn't literally store coins the way a physical wallet stores cash — it stores the keys that prove ownership and let you move funds on the blockchain. Who actually holds those keys is the single most important distinction between different kinds of wallets.

highlights.text: stores the keys that prove ownership

blocks.body: A custodial wallet is one where a third party, typically a cryptocurrency exchange, holds the keys on your behalf. You log in with a username and password, much like a bank account, and the company handles the technical side. That convenience comes with a real catch: you're trusting that company to keep your funds safe, stay solvent, and let you withdraw whenever you want.

blocks.robotComment: Full control and full responsibility arrive as a package deal here. 🎒
blocks.body: A non-custodial wallet, sometimes called a self-custody wallet, is one where you alone hold the keys, often as software on your own phone or computer, or on a dedicated hardware device. Nobody else can freeze or access your funds without your keys — but that also means there's no company to call and no password reset if you lose access yourself.

highlights.text: no company to call and no password reset

blocks.sentence: A wallet where a third party like an exchange holds your keys on your behalf is called a ___ wallet.
blocks.explanation: Custodial means a third party is in custody of your keys, similar to how a bank holds your money.

blocks.question: What's the key practical difference between a custodial and a non-custodial wallet?
options: Who holds the keys — a third party in a custodial wallet, versus only you in a non-custodial wallet
Custodial wallets are just non-custodial wallets under a different name
Non-custodial wallets are run entirely by banks
There is no meaningful difference between the two
blocks.explanation: Custody of the keys — third party versus yourself alone — is the defining difference, and it drives most of the risk and convenience tradeoffs.

blocks.statement: With a non-custodial wallet, if you lose your own access, there's typically no company able to reset it for you.
blocks.explanation: Full control over a non-custodial wallet also means full responsibility — there's usually no customer support line able to recover it.
blocks.robotComment: Keep this one in mind — it matters a lot for the next two lessons. 🧭
The names genuinely describe the whole idea: one is meant to be public, the other must stay private. 🗝️
blocks.body: Underneath every wallet are two related pieces of cryptography: a public key and a private key. Think of the public key as similar to an account number you can safely share with anyone so they can send you funds, and the private key as similar to the password that actually authorizes spending them — except a private key must never be shared with anyone, ever.

When you send cryptocurrency, your wallet uses your private key to create a digital signature proving the transaction really came from you, without ever revealing the private key itself. The rest of the network can check that signature using your public key, confirming it's genuine, all without you ever having to hand over your actual password-equivalent.

highlights.text: without ever revealing the private key itself

blocks.robotComment: Write it down on paper, store it somewhere safe and offline, and never type it into a website that asks for it out of nowhere. ⚠️
blocks.body: In practice, most wallets represent your private key as a recovery phrase: a sequence of 12 or 24 ordinary-looking words, generated when you first set up the wallet. That phrase is the master key to your funds — anyone who obtains it can access and move everything in the wallet, and if you permanently lose it with no backup, the funds are typically gone for good.

highlights.text: the funds are typically gone for good

blocks.sentence: The piece of information that must never be shared and is used to authorize spending is called your ___ key.
blocks.explanation: The private key authorizes spending and must stay secret; the public key is safe to share so others can send you funds.

blocks.question: What is a private key used for?
options: Creating a digital signature that authorizes spending, without ever being shared publicly
Being posted publicly so anyone can find your wallet
Only receiving funds, never sending them
Nothing — it's a decorative label with no real function
blocks.explanation: A private key authorizes spending by creating a signature — it must stay secret, unlike a public key.

blocks.statement: It's generally safe to share your wallet's recovery phrase with a website that asks for it to help you.
blocks.explanation: A legitimate service never needs your recovery phrase — sharing it is one of the most common ways people lose their funds entirely.
blocks.robotComment: If anything ever asks for that phrase unprompted, treat it as an immediate red flag. 🚩

lessons.title: Why "Not Your Keys, Not Your Coins" Is a Real Warning

blocks.robotComment: Harsh-sounding, but it's really just describing a specific, well-documented risk. 🧭
blocks.body: You'll often hear the phrase "not your keys, not your coins" in cryptocurrency spaces. It's blunt, but it's pointing at something real: when you leave cryptocurrency sitting on an exchange instead of a wallet where you hold the private keys yourself, you don't fully control it — the exchange does, in practice.

highlights.text: not your keys, not your coins

blocks.body: This isn't hypothetical caution. Cryptocurrency exchanges have failed, frozen withdrawals, or been hacked before, and when that happens, customers holding funds on that exchange can lose access to some or all of it — sometimes permanently. Holding your own keys removes that particular risk, because no exchange's problems can touch funds it never actually held.

highlights.text: lose access to some or all of it
no exchange's problems can touch funds it never actually held

blocks.robotComment: Custodial risk and self-custody risk are both real — the point is knowing which one you're accepting, not that one is always right. ⚖️
blocks.body: But self-custody isn't automatically the safer choice for everyone, and it's worth being honest about that too. If you lose your private key or recovery phrase, there's typically no customer support to call and no way to recover the funds — ever. A careless mistake with self-custody can be just as final as an exchange failure, just from a different cause.

highlights.text: self-custody isn't automatically the safer choice for everyone
just as final as an exchange failure

blocks.sentence: The phrase "not your keys, not your ___" warns that funds left on an exchange aren't fully in your control.
blocks.explanation: The saying is a reminder that whoever holds the private keys, not just whoever's name is on the account, has practical control of the funds.

blocks.question: What is the honest, balanced takeaway about custodial versus self-custody risk?
options: Both carry real risk — exchange failure or hacks on one side, unrecoverable personal mistakes on the other — and neither is automatically the safer choice for everyone
Keeping funds on an exchange is always completely risk-free
Neither option carries any risk at all
blocks.explanation: This is a genuine tradeoff between two different kinds of risk, not a case where one option is safe and the other is dangerous.

blocks.statement: If you lose a self-custody wallet's private key with no backup, there's typically a company able to recover the funds for you.
blocks.explanation: Self-custody means no company holds a backup — losing the key or recovery phrase with no backup is typically permanent and unrecoverable.
